title: What Happens When You Press Send on WhatsApp

youtube.title: What Really Happens When You Press Send on WhatsApp (Explained Simply)
youtube.summary: You tap send and a grey tick appears in a blink. In that moment your phone locks the message with a brand new key, sends it through an encrypted tunnel to WhatsApp's servers, and the server passes on a box it cannot open. In this video we follow one message: the keys your phone makes when you install WhatsApp, how two phones agree on a secret even when one is offline, why every message gets a new key, what the grey and blue ticks really mean, how photos and group chats are handled, and how long the server keeps your message.
youtube.details:
Key figures (checked November 2026):
- About 100 billion messages a day (Mark Zuckerberg, Facebook Q3 2020 earnings call)
- More than 3 billion monthly users (Mark Zuckerberg, Meta Q1 2025 earnings call)
- Keys: identity key, signed pre key and one-time pre keys (Curve25519); only public halves are uploaded (WhatsApp Security Whitepaper)
- Session setup combines four key exchanges into a master secret; works while the recipient is offline
- Each message key is 80 bytes: 32-byte AES-256 key, 32-byte HMAC-SHA256 key, 16-byte IV; keys ratchet forward after every message
- Media: encrypted with a random key, uploaded as an encrypted blob; the key travels inside the message
- Groups: sender keys; message encrypted once, server fans it out
- Delivered messages are deleted from the servers; undelivered ones are kept encrypted for up to 30 days (WhatsApp Privacy Policy)

How WhatsApp sends a photo it can't see

scenes.sub: about 100 billion a day, by Mark Zuckerberg's own count
scenes.text: You type a message, tap send, and a little grey tick appears almost instantly. It feels like nothing. But WhatsApp handles around one hundred billion messages every single day, and every one of them goes through the same hidden routine. Before your message even leaves your phone, it is locked. It travels to WhatsApp's servers, but the server cannot read it. And the key that locked it is used for that one message only, then thrown away. By the end of this video, you will know exactly what happens in the second after you press send, what the ticks really mean, and why even WhatsApp cannot open your chats.

scenes.chapterTitle: Open padlocks at the post office

items.text: Your friend leaves open padlocks at the post office
You lock your letter in a box with one
Only your friend has the key

footer.text: The post office carries a box

scenes.text: Here is a simple way to picture it. Imagine your friend goes to the post office and leaves a pile of open padlocks there. Anyone can take one and snap it shut, but only your friend has the key that opens them. When you want to send a private letter, you pick up one of those padlocks, put your letter in a box, and lock it. Now the post office carries the box to your friend. The postman can see the box, who sent it and where it is going, but he cannot open it. Only your friend can. WhatsApp works in a very similar way, except the padlocks and keys are made of maths, and the whole thing happens in a fraction of a second.

scenes.chapterTitle: The four stops of a message

items.name: Your phone
items.desc: Locks the message before it leaves

items.name: Secure tunnel
items.desc: A second layer of encryption to the server

items.name: WhatsApp server
items.desc: Passes on a box it cannot open

items.name: Friend's phone
items.desc: The only place it gets unlocked

scenes.text: So let us follow one message on its journey. It has four stops. First, your phone, where the message is locked before it goes anywhere. Second, a secure tunnel. Your phone talks to WhatsApp through its own encrypted connection, so the locked box is wrapped in a second layer of protection while it travels. Third, the WhatsApp server, which works like the post office. It reads the address and passes the box along. And fourth, your friend's phone, the only place where the message is ever unlocked. This is what end to end encryption means. The message is locked at one end and opened at the other, and nothing in the middle can read it.

scenes.chapterTitle: What happens when you install WhatsApp

items.text: Your phone makes its own key pairs
Public halves go to the server
Private halves never leave your phone
A stack of one-time keys waits for senders

scenes.text: The padlocks are created long before you send anything. When you install WhatsApp, your phone generates several key pairs. Each pair has two halves. A public half, which works like an open padlock, and a private half, which is the only key that can open it. Your phone keeps a long term identity key, a signed key that is replaced from time to time, and a whole stack of one time keys. It uploads only the public halves to WhatsApp's server. The private halves never leave your phone. So the server only ever sees the open padlocks. It never holds the keys that open them.

scenes.chapterTitle: How two phones agree on a secret

items.text: Your phone downloads your friend's public keys
It mixes them with a fresh key of its own
Four calculations give one shared secret
Works even if your friend is offline

scenes.text: Now, the first time you message someone, your phone needs to agree on a secret with theirs. It downloads your friend's public keys from the server, including one of those one time keys, which the server then deletes so it is never used twice. Your phone also creates a fresh key of its own and mixes everything together. It runs four separate calculations and combines them into one shared secret. Your friend's phone can later do the same maths with its private keys and arrive at exactly the same secret. And here is the clever part. The secret itself is never sent across the internet. And because the keys were waiting on the server, this works even if your friend is offline.

From that shared secret, your phone creates a message key. It is eighty bytes long, and it has three parts. The first thirty two bytes are an A E S two fifty six key, which scrambles the text so it looks like random noise. The next thirty two bytes are used to create a seal, a kind of digital fingerprint that proves nothing was changed on the way. And the last sixteen bytes are a random starting point for the scrambling. If anyone tried to change even one letter of your locked message while it travelled, the seal breaks, and your friend's phone would simply reject it.

scenes.chapterTitle: Why every message gets a new key

items.text: Each message key is used once
The next key is made from the last one
Old keys are deleted
Each reply adds fresh randomness

footer.text: Steal one key and you get

scenes.text: Here is something most people never realise. Every message you send gets its own brand new key. Each message key is used once. Then your phone runs the old chain through a one way calculation to make the next key, and the old key is deleted. It is like a ratchet that only turns forward. On top of that, every time your friend sends a reply, both phones mix in fresh random keys, so the chain keeps changing direction. Why bother? Because if someone ever managed to steal one key, they would unlock one message, not your whole chat history. Security experts call this forward secrecy.

items.name: One grey tick
items.desc: Sent: the server has your locked message

items.name: Two blue ticks
items.desc: Your friend has opened the chat

chips.text: Not delivered: kept up to 30 days

footer.highlight: a waiting room, not an archive

scenes.text: Now let us decode the ticks. One grey tick means your message was sent. It has left your phone and reached WhatsApp's server. Two grey ticks mean it was delivered to your friend's phone. And two blue ticks mean your friend has opened the chat and read it. But what happens to the copy on the server? According to WhatsApp's privacy policy, once a message is delivered, it is deleted from their servers. If your friend's phone is switched off, the locked message waits, and WhatsApp keeps trying for up to thirty days. After that, it is deleted. So the server is a waiting room, not an archive.

items.text: Your phone makes a random key for the file
The locked file is uploaded
The key travels inside your message
Your friend downloads and unlocks it

scenes.text: Photos and videos are much bigger than text, so they take a slightly different route. When you send a photo, your phone first creates a random key just for that file and locks the photo with it. The locked file is then uploaded to WhatsApp's storage. Next, your phone sends your friend a normal encrypted message containing three things. Where the file is, the key that opens it, and a fingerprint to check it has not been changed. Your friend's phone downloads the locked file and unlocks it. The server stores a file it cannot see, and the key travels inside a message it cannot read.

items.title: Encrypt
items.sub: your phone locks the message one time

chips.text: Someone leaves? New keys for everyone

scenes.text: What about group chats? Locking the same message separately for two hundred people would drain your battery. So WhatsApp uses a trick called sender keys. The first time you write in a group, your phone creates a special sender key and shares it privately with each member, using the one to one locks we just talked about. After that, your phone locks each group message just one time. The server makes copies and delivers one to every member, and they all unlock it with your sender key. And whenever someone leaves the group, everyone throws away their old keys and starts fresh. It is faster for you, and still unreadable for the server.

items.text: Your phone locks the message before it leaves
The server passes on a box it cannot open
Every message gets a brand new key

scenes.text: Let us recap in three points. One. When you press send, your phone locks the message using keys that were set up between you and your friend, and the private keys never leave your phones. Two. The locked message travels through a secure tunnel to WhatsApp's server, which passes on a box it cannot open, and deletes it once it is delivered. Three. Every message gets a brand new key, so even if one key was ever stolen, the rest of your chat stays safe. Sending a single message is a tiny feat of maths, repeated billions of times a day.
